en: The Sūtra on Ultimate Emptiness Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma (Shi Hu), Dharma Master and Imperial Preceptor of the Great Song,
recipient of the purple robe and the title of Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and others, by imperial decree.
At one time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying in the kingdom of Kuru together with a community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"As for all the dharma-gates, I have already explained them as before."
Furthermore, there is a true Dharma called "Emptiness of the Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha-śūnyatā). Listen attentively and apply your minds with great care;
I shall now explain it for you. "O Bhikṣus!
In this context, what is called "emptiness of the ultimate" (paramārtha-śūnyatā)?
It means that when the eye arises, there is not even the slightest dharma from which it comes.
Furthermore, when the eye ceases, there is not even the slightest dharma that disperses or departs. "O Bhikṣus!
That eye is without reality; it is devoid of any real dharma."
To state it briefly:
there is karma and there is its retribution, yet no agent can be found; once these aggregates have ended, one is again comprised of other aggregates;
these are a collection of distinct phenomena, produced by causes and conditions.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
When that mind arises, not even the slightest dharma comes from anywhere;
and when the mind ceases, not even the slightest dharma disperses or goes away.
“O Bhikṣus! That mind is without reality and is devoid of real dharmas; as previously stated, it is a collection of distinct dharmas.
This dharma of collection cannot be found to have any reality; it is produced by causes and conditions.”
This dependent origination is as follows: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations;

conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. Thus does this entire great mass of suffering arise.
These phenomena that arise have no substantial reality that can be apprehended;

having arisen, they immediately perish. Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
What has been explained in this manner is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). "O Bhikṣus!
All the Dharma-gates that have already been explained previously—this true Dharma, you should now study."
The Sūtra on Ultimate Emptiness Spoken by the Buddha
